window: 60-minute duration-matched runs (a 5-min run agrees) at the 3.5× bloatnet (perf-devnet-3, head 24,358,000) on state-vm-1, under live head + 50 concurrent Locust read clients. Nethermind master (1.40.0-unstable) vs Geth master; overlay isolation; mock-CL replay of blocks 24,358,001+. 0 RPC failures on either client (587k / 595k requests over the hour).
proofParity: eth_getProof byte sizes are near-identical across clients — p50 8,071 B (NM) vs 8,072 B (Geth), mean 10,912 B on both — exactly as expected for the same state root. EIP-1186 proofs are client-agnostic, so the witness-size metric is comparable regardless of which client serves it.
summary: Matched over a full hour against the same 3.5× state and read load, the two clients land at opposite optima. Geth wins read-serving decisively: aggregate p99 22 ms vs 160 ms (~7×), mean 1.6 ms vs 5.8 ms, tight and uniform across all five methods — on ~18 GB peak RSS vs Nethermind's ~57 GB (~3×). Nethermind wins execution: it advances ~1.7× more blocks under live head (3,670 vs 2,108 over the hour), pushes ~2,014 vs 816 Mgas/s average (~2.5×) with faster per-block processing, and keeps a smaller on-disk DB (1.80 vs 2.34 TB) — but pays for it in memory and disk I/O (697 vs 264 MB/s peak). Both clients' memory stayed bounded over the hour. Net: Geth optimizes for cheap, low-latency state reads with a small footprint; Nethermind trades memory + disk I/O for higher block/gas execution throughput.
caveat: Block-processing time and gas/s are NOT a strict like-for-like statistic — Geth reports a decaying go-metrics timer (chain_execution / chain_mgasps) while Nethermind reports gauges (last_block_processing_time / mgas_per_sec); blocks-advanced and gas/s are the steadier execution comparison. The read window (recent_block_window=64) sits inside both clients' served-state window, so latency is fair — but it doesn't exercise Nethermind's deeper-history advantage (FlatDb tunable vs Geth pathdb's fixed ~128-block window). Besu / Reth / Erigon pending per issues #21 / #26.
note: Cross-client read + execution battery from issue #21 (5-min + 60-min runs). Besu / Reth / Erigon and the higher milestones land in benchmarks/<milestone>/ as produced.

x5.window: 5-minute WORK-matched run at the 5× bloatnet (perf-devnet-3, head 24,546,596) on state-vm-2 — Geth advanced 136 blocks, Nethermind 142, so both did comparable import work. Geth v1.17.4 (chainId-12159-patched) vs Nethermind master; overlay isolation; mock-CL replay of blocks 24,546,597+. 0 RPC failures (48.9k / 47.5k requests).
x5.summary: At 5×, work-matched over the same ~140-block replay, the x3.5 picture holds: Geth serves reads with a ~3× lower tail (aggregate p99 110 ms vs 360 ms, mean 3.7 ms vs 12.8 ms) on ~2.4× lighter memory (28.7 GB vs 69.1 GB peak); Nethermind pushes ~3× the gas throughput (4,469 vs 1,480 Mgas/s) and keeps a ~27% smaller DB (2.23 vs 3.06 TB). eth_getProof bytes are identical across clients (mean ~11.4 KB).
x5.workMatched: The 5-minute numbers above are the fair read-latency comparison because both clients did comparable work. In the 60-minute run they did NOT: Geth accelerated to 1,278 blocks while Nethermind (under memory pressure — RSS climbed past 170 GB) throttled its own replay to 561, so Geth executed ~2.3× the work and far heavier blocks by the end. Under that load its read tail rose (last-10-min p99 528 ms vs Nethermind's 181 ms), while at the equal-work 5-minute mark Geth's tail (~110–197 ms) sat well below Nethermind's (~360 ms). Read latency here is coupled to import duty cycle — the honest cross-client statement is per-unit-of-work, where Geth stays the lighter, lower-tail reader and Nethermind the higher-throughput executor. A block-count-capped run is the open item that fully decouples the two.
